short.headline: India’s Population Pyramid Is Narrowing at the Base
short.dek: Child share down from 35.6% in 2000 to 22.4% by 2030; median age to nearly double by 2100.
short.body: India's population pyramid is reshaping from a wide-based triangle to a rectangular column. In 2000, over a third of Indians were below 15. By 2030, that share will fall to less than a quarter. The working-age bulk is swelling, pushing the median age from 21.19 to a projected 47.78 by century's end. This shift carries huge implications for schools, jobs, and elder care. The data comes from UN World Population Prospects, the most widely used demographic dataset.

macha.heading: Chalo, what’s the real story, yaar?
macha.body: For decades, India was a young country—almost every family had many small kids. Now, that’s changing fast. The bottom of the pyramid is shrinking because families are having fewer babies. The middle is bulging with young adults entering the workforce. This is a once-in-a-lifetime advantage: fewer mouths to feed per working hand. But don’t get too comfortable. Those young adults will grow old, and soon we’ll have many more grandparents to care for. The pyramid is flipping from a children’s party to an elders’ ki dukaan. So, enjoy the demographic dividend while it lasts, because the bill for old-age will come due in a few decades.
macha.soWhat: India’s demographic dividend is here, but the window is closing as the population ages.

article.title: What does India's population pyramid look like?
article.standfirst: India’s population pyramid is losing its wide base. The share of children has plunged from 35.6% in 2000 to a projected 22.4% by 2030, while the working-age core swells. The median age will nearly double by 2100. These projections reshape how we think about schools, jobs, and elder care.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## What is the headline answer?

India’s population pyramid is no longer a true pyramid. Its shape is shifting from a wide-based triangle to a more rectangular column. In 2000, children under 15 made up 35.6% of India. That was more than one in three people. By 2030, the share of children is projected to fall to 22.4%. This sharp fall signals the end of India’s extremely youthful age structure. The working-age share is swelling, and the median age is climbing. In 2000, the median Indian was 21.19 years old. By the end of this century, UN projections suggest that halfway mark will reach 47.78 years. The pyramid’s transformation is one of the most far‑reaching changes happening in India today.

## What exactly is being measured?

The population pyramid is a bar chart that shows how many people are in each 5‑year age group, with males on the left and females on the right. The bar lengths represent the number of people, not percentages. In 2030, the largest group will be the 20‑24 year‑olds at 12.5 crore. The 0‑4 age group will be 11.1 crore, smaller than the 20‑24 and 15‑19 (12.3 crore) groups. This bulge in the young‑adult ages is the hallmark of a country that has passed through the first phase of the demographic transition, where fertility has fallen but past high fertility still echoes in large adult cohorts. To measure the economic burden, demographers use the dependency ratio: the number of people outside working age (0‑14 and 65+) for every 100 people aged 15‑64. In 2000, the total dependency ratio was 66.57. By 2030, it is projected to be 44.81, a dramatic fall that creates a so‑called ‘demographic dividend’. The median age confirms the shift: half the population was below 21.19 in 2000, and projections for 2100 push that to 47.78.

## How should a normal reader read the chart?

Start by looking at the silhouette. The pyramid has two halves, left for males and right for females. The vertical axis lists age bands, from 0‑4 at the bottom to 80+ at the top. Each bar stretches outwards; the longer the bar, the more people in that group. In a classic young‑country pyramid, the 0‑4 bar is the widest. But in India’s 2030 pyramid, the 0‑4 bar (11.1 crore) is already shorter than the bars for people aged 15‑19 (12.3 crore) and 20‑24 (12.5 crore). This means there are more teenagers and young adults than little children. Compare with the 2000 pyramid: although we do not have the exact bar‑by‑bar counts here, the overall shape was a smooth triangle with a very wide base. The 2030 shape is more like a barrel. When reading the chart, watch for two things: how wide the base is (it tells you about recent births) and where the bulge sits (it tells you which generation is largest). The bulge moves upwards over time as that large cohort ages.

## What comparison or breakdown changes the meaning?

The falling total dependency ratio sounds like good news: from 66.57 in 2000 to 44.81 in 2030. But this number hides a critical shift. The child dependency ratio has fallen sharply, from 59.22 in 2000 to 32.42 in 2030. At the same time, the old‑age dependency ratio is rising, from 7.35 to 12.39 over the same period. So, while the total burden on workers is declining, the type of burden is changing: fewer mouths to feed, more grandparents to support. The child dependency drop accounts for nearly all the decline in the total ratio. The old‑age ratio, though still modest, is on an upward path that will only accelerate. This means the ‘demographic dividend’ phase is finite. Once the large working‑age cohorts grow older, the total dependency ratio will start rising again, perhaps by mid‑century. The breakdown shows that India’s dependency profile is being reshaped from one dominated by children to one that will eventually have as many or more elderly dependents.

## What does the number not tell us?

All the numbers for 2030 and beyond are projections, not facts. They rely on assumptions about how quickly fertility will fall and how long people will live. The median projection we cite, median age reaching 47.78 by 2100, is the UN’s middle scenario. But the UN also runs other scenarios. In a high‑fertility world, the median age in 2100 would be 39.38. In a low‑fertility world, it would be 57.73. So the future age structure could be 10 years younger or older than the baseline. These are national averages. They hide enormous diversity: southern states are aging rapidly, while northern states still have higher birth rates. The dependency ratios themselves use rigid age cutoffs: 15‑64 for working age. In reality, many 65‑year‑olds work, and many people in their early 20s are in college. So the economic burden is not captured perfectly. Finally, the pyramid does not always show the sex ratio within age groups, a dimension that matters in India.

## What should the reader remember?

India’s population pyramid is in the middle of a historic shift. It is transitioning from a young, broad‑based shape to an older, more rectangular one. The median age has already doubled from 21.19 in 2000 to a projected 47.78 by 2100. The total dependency ratio of 44.81 per 100 workers in 2030 is a low point that offers a window of opportunity. But this window will not stay open forever. The old‑age dependency ratio, now at 12.39, will climb relentlessly. Eventually, the total dependency will bottom out and rise again, raising questions about pension systems, healthcare, and the size of the future workforce. The key takeaway is simple: India is no longer a country of children; it is a country in mid‑life, heading towards old age. The speed of this transition will determine how well the country manages its demographic dividend today and its silver dividend tomorrow.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Think of a birthday-party photograph where everyone is lined up by age, youngest on the floor, oldest on chairs. A population pyramid is a bar chart that does exactly that for a whole country. It splits the population into age groups (usually 5-year bands) and shows the number of males on the left side and females on the right. The shape tells you if a country is young (wide base, like a triangle) or old (narrow base, like a rectangle). It counts people, not percentages, so the total width can grow over time. It doesn't show the exact number of people in each age group per square kilometre, only the absolute count.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The shape of India’s pyramid is the direct answer to the question. A narrowing base and a bulging middle reveal the shift from a young to an aging population.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Picture a joint family where some members earn and others do not. The dependency ratio counts how many 'non-earners' (children under 15 and elders above 64) there are for every 100 'potential workers' (ages 15 to 64). It is a rough measure of the economic burden on the working-age group. A ratio of 50 means 50 dependents per 100 working-age people. It does not mean those 50 actually depend on those 100; many elderly still work, and many young adults study. The ratio simply uses age cutoffs, not actual employment status.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's total dependency ratio is falling, but the composition is shifting from children to the elderly. This change will determine future needs for schools, jobs, and elder care.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: If you line up every person in India from youngest to oldest, the median age is the age of the person standing exactly in the middle. It splits the population into two equal halves: one younger, one older. A median age of 21 means half the country is below 21; a median age of 47 means half is below 47. It is not the average age, but a midpoint that is very sensitive to the number of children. So, a falling birth rate pulls the median age up.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The median age gives a single, easy-to-grasp number that tracks how fast India is aging. It is projected to more than double by 2100.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A projection is a 'what-if' calculation, not a crystal ball. Demographers take current birth and death rates and make assumptions about how they will change. Then they run the numbers forward. If fertility falls faster than assumed, the population will be older than the projection. It is like planning a family budget assuming your salary will grow 5% each year; if you get a bigger hike, the budget changes. Projections are always uncertain, especially far into the future.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All the numbers for 2030 and 2100 are projections. Small changes in fertility can shift the median age by several years, as shown by the high and low scenarios.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Instead of looking at every 5-year age band, demographers often group ages into three big buckets: children (0-14), working-age (15-64), and elderly (65+). This simplification helps us see the big picture. It’s like sorting a bus full of passengers into school kids, office-goers, and senior citizens. The share of each group tells you what stage of life the country is in.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Broad age group shares in 2000 and 2030 show directly how the child share is shrinking and the working-age share is swelling, even as the total population grows.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: This is the United Nations’ official dataset that estimates and projects the population of every country using a consistent method. It is based on censuses, surveys, and vital registration data. The UN publishes updates every few years, and its numbers are used by governments and researchers worldwide. It is not an Indian government source, but it is the most widely cited global demographic database.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All the charts and numbers on this page come from the UN World Population Prospects. It provides the age-sex breakdown needed to build the pyramid and the dependency ratios.

chartExplainers.title: Population by 5-year age groups and sex
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2030, the largest age group is 20-24 year olds at 12.5 crore, while the 0-4 group is only 11.1 crore, showing a narrower base.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart displays two population pyramids side by side, one for 2000 and one for 2030. Each bar represents a 5-year age group, with males on the left and females on the right. In 2000, the shape was a classic pyramid: wide at the bottom (0-4) and narrowing as age increased. By 2030, the base has shrunk significantly. The 0-4 age group in 2030 is 11.1 crore, compared to 12.5 crore in the 20-24 age group. The middle of the chart bulges because the large cohorts born in the 1990s and early 2000s are now young adults. The 15-19 group is 12.3 crore. The pyramid shows India's demographic transition in a single snapshot: fewer babies, more workers.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The pyramid directly answers the page question by showing the age and sex structure.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the lengths of the bars: a wide bar means a large population in that age group. The shape tells the age story.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the bars as percentages; they show absolute numbers, so the total size of the pyramid grows over time.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep it full-width with minimal labels for mobile.

chartExplainers.title: Percentage of total population by broad age group
chartExplainers.takeaway: The share of children (0-14) has fallen from 35.6% in 2000 to 22.4% in 2030.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart breaks the population into age groups 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, showing how shares have changed between 2000 and 2030. In 2000, children made up 35.6% of India, while the working-age (15-64) took most of the remaining share and the elderly only a small fraction. By 2030, children drop to 22.4% and the working-age share rises to absorb the difference. The elderly share also grows modestly, though it remains under 10%. This shift is the essence of the demographic transition: a smaller base and a larger middle.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It simplifies the pyramid into three age groups, highlighting the big picture shift.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar represents 100%, split into segments. Compare the children segment across years to see the decline.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A falling share does not necessarily mean the absolute number is falling; it could still grow if total population grows fast enough.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use horizontal bars for easy label reading.

chartExplainers.title: Total dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: The total dependency ratio has fallen from 66.57 dependents per 100 working-age people in 2000 to 44.81 by 2030.
chartExplainers.detail: The total dependency ratio adds together children (0-14) and elderly (65+) and divides by the working-age population (15-64). A lower number means fewer dependents per worker. India's ratio has declined steeply as birth rates fell. In 2000, for every 100 people of working age, there were 66.57 dependents, mostly children. By 2030, that burden drops to 44.81, the lowest in India's modern history. This creates a 'demographic dividend' phase where a larger share of the population can work and save. However, the ratio will start rising again after mid-century as the large working-age cohorts retire.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It quantifies the support burden on the working-age population.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A ratio of 44.81 means about 45 dependents per 100 workers. Look for the trend line declining.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't equate dependency with actual economic dependency; many people over 65 still work, and many 15-64 are students or unemployed.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a line chart with clear annual ticks.

chartExplainers.title: Median age of population
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's median age is projected to rise from 21.19 years in 2000 to 47.78 years by 2100.
chartExplainers.detail: The median age is the age that splits the population into equal halves. In 2000, half of India was below 21.19, a hallmark of a very young country. But this is rising rapidly. By 2100, the median is projected to reach 47.78 years, meaning half the population will be over 47. This rise is driven by falling fertility and longer lives. Under the low-fertility scenario, the median could reach 57.73, and even under high fertility, it would reach 39.38. The chart shows a steady upward climb, with no signs of slowing down. This has profound implications for healthcare, pensions, and labor supply.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A single number that captures the entire aging trend.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the line climb over the century; the steeper the slope, the faster the aging.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A rising median age does not mean everyone is old; it means there are fewer young children pulling the median down.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A line chart with sparse labels works well on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: Child dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: Child dependency has nearly halved, from 59.22 per 100 working-age in 2000 to 32.42 in 2030.
chartExplainers.detail: The child dependency ratio measures the number of children (0-14) relative to the working-age population (15-64). In 2000, there were 59.22 child dependents for every 100 potential workers. By 2030, that number drops to 32.42, reflecting the dramatic decline in birth rates. This reduction is the main driver behind the falling total dependency ratio. It means less pressure on schools and child-related services, and potentially more resources available per child. But it also means that in the future, the workforce will grow more slowly, and eventually may shrink.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Isolates the young dependent burden, which is the biggest part of the dependency story.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A declining line indicates fewer children per worker over time.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This number can fall even if the absolute number of children is stable, because the denominator (working-age population) is growing.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple line chart with clear axis labels.

chartExplainers.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: Old-age dependency is rising, from 7.35 in 2000 to 12.39 in 2030, and will accelerate.
chartExplainers.detail: The old-age dependency ratio compares the elderly (65+) to the working-age population (15-64). In 2000, it was just 7.35 per 100. By 2030, it reaches 12.39, still low but growing. This ratio will increase sharply after 2040 as the large cohorts born in the 1970s and 1980s enter old age. By 2100, it could surpass the child dependency ratio in many states. The rising burden will require more spending on pensions, healthcare, and elder care. The chart shows a slow initial climb that steepens over time.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Highlights the emerging challenge of an aging population.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line starts low but curves upward; the steepness after 2030 indicates the speed of aging.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Even though this ratio is still low, its growth rate is what matters for planning.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a line chart with a log or linear scale appropriately.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A bar chart that shows the number of people in each age group, with males on the left and females on the right, giving it a pyramid shape when the population is young.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The shape of the pyramid directly answers whether India is young, working-age, or aging.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of people who are typically not in the labor force (children under 15 and adults over 64) divided by the working-age population (15-64), multiplied by 100. It measures the support burden on workers.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It tells us how many dependents each worker supports, and the composition shift from children to elderly defines India's future economic and social needs.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The age that splits the population exactly in half. If a country has a median age of 25, there are as many people younger than 25 as older than 25.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It gives a single number to track how fast India is aging, from 21 in 2000 to a projected 48 by 2100.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: An estimate of future population based on assumptions about births, deaths, and migration. It is not a prediction but a 'what-if' scenario.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: All the 2030 and 2100 figures are projections, so they depend on how many children women have in the coming decades, which can change.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A simplified grouping of ages, usually 0-14 (children), 15-64 (working-age), and 65+ (elderly). Some definitions use different cutoffs.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: These groups let us see the big picture shift from a young population to an older one without getting lost in 5-year details.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The official United Nations dataset that estimates past populations and projects future populations for every country, using a consistent method so numbers are comparable across countries.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It is the most widely used source for population structure data and the basis for all figures on this page.

proseRules: No calculations unless the evidence packet supplies the derived number

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
